newsitem.title: USA: Bill introduced on Hong Kong journalists.
newsitem.headline: Bill introduced on Hong Kong journalists.

text.p: A bill to provide up to 2,000 U.S. visas for Hong Kong journalists after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control this year was introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives on Thursday.

Representative John Porter, an Illinois Republican, who introduced the bill, said it was intended to send a message in support of press freedom in Hong Kong to China, which will take control of the British colony at midnight on June 30.

Porter is co-chairman of the Congressional Human Rights Caucus and the Hong Kong caucus. He visited Hong Kong last month and said many journalists told him they were fearful about what might happen to them when China assumes power.

"We are already seeing pressure and self-censorship creeping into journalism in Hong Kong," Porter said in a statement. "This legislation would provide a safety net for journalists in Hong Kong, so they can continue to do their jobs without fear of reprisal or retribution."
The visas would be available to journalists of Hong Kong or Chinese nationality who have worked in the Hong Kong media for at least three years and their immediate family members.
The U.S. consul general in Hong Kong said earlier that the United States was concerned about press freedom and free elections for the local legislature when China takes control.

Richard Boucher said the United States felt that China was living up to its promises on many aspects of its planned takeover but there were questions about how long a provisional Beijing-backed legislature would remain in control and about the future of a free press.
"We have some important concerns," Boucher said at the National Press Club.

He said Hong Kong's press "has already been limited by self-censorship," for fear of offending China's leadership. "Some editors say privately they fear losing advertising revenue" if they do not toe the line, he added.
Boucher also said that the United States wanted to see free elections for the former British colony's legislature as soon as possible.
He said he hoped China would use the takeover as "an opportunity to show that it lives up to its commitments."
"It is a basically positive picture," he said of China's handling of the takeover, "but we have some serious reservations."
